body:
Meaning of Gujarati Rangbhumi

Gujarati Rangbhumi refers to the tradition of theatrical performance in the Gujarati language. It includes traditional folk theatre, professional drama companies, literary plays, amateur theatre and modern commercial and experimental productions.

Theatre is a composite performing art because it brings together literature, acting, dialogue, music, dance, costumes and other forms of artistic expression. In Gujarat, theatre has historically served both entertainment and social education.

The development of Gujarati theatre cannot be understood solely through written plays. Gujarat possessed an established tradition of folk performance long before the emergence of organised theatre companies in the 19th century.

Bhavai: The traditional foundation

Bhavai is a traditional folk theatre form of Gujarat, particularly associated with North Gujarat. Its origin is traditionally attributed to Asait Thakar, who lived in the 14th century and is associated with Siddhpur and Unjha.

Bhavai developed as a form of religious and community performance but gradually incorporated subjects drawn from ordinary social life. Its humour and satire exposed hypocrisy, caste discrimination, exploitation, inappropriate marriages and other social problems.

Important features of Bhavai

  • Vesha: An individual dramatic episode or short play within a Bhavai performance.
  • Chachar: The open performance space, traditionally located in a village square or temple courtyard.
  • Bhungal: A long wind instrument closely associated with Bhavai performances.
  • Ranglo: A comic character who entertains the audience and comments on social behaviour. Rangli also appears in later forms of presentation.
  • Nayak: The leader of a traditional performing troupe.
  • Bhavaiya: A traditional Bhavai performer. The Targala community has historically been closely associated with this art.

Bhavai traditionally combines dialogue, singing, dancing and humour without requiring elaborate stage buildings or painted scenery. Historically, male performers also played female characters.

Its religious association is particularly strong with the worship of the Mother Goddess, Amba. However, its dramatic subjects are not exclusively religious.

Important Bhavai veshas

VeshaPrincipal association
Jasma OdanA folk legend concerning courage, dignity and fidelity
KajodaSatire on mismatched marriages
RamdevReligious and devotional tradition
Jhanda JhulanTraditional dramatic episode

Tradition credits Asait Thakar with composing approximately 360 veshas. This is a traditional attribution, not the number of surviving or independently authenticated scripts.

From folk theatre to organised theatre

During the 19th century, Gujarati theatre developed through interaction between Bhavai, Sanskrit dramatic traditions, Western theatre and the Parsi stage of Bombay, now Mumbai.

The emergence of written scripts, permanent theatres and professional companies did not eliminate Bhavai. Folk theatre continued alongside organised theatre and later became an important source of inspiration for modern Gujarati playwrights and directors.

Prelims focus

  • Asait Thakar is traditionally regarded as the founder of Bhavai.
  • Bhavai is associated with the 14th century and North Gujarat.
  • Vesha is a dramatic episode; Bhungal is a musical instrument.
  • Ranglo is associated with humour and social commentary.
  • Kajoda deals with mismatched marriages.
  • Trap: Bhavai is a folk theatre form, not merely a folk dance.

[References: NCERT, Class 11, Living Craft Traditions of India, Chapter 10, Theatre Crafts, printed pp. 113 and 117; Gujarat State School Textbook Board, Class 10, Social Science, Chapter 2, Cultural Heritage of India: Traditional Handicraft and Fine Arts, printed pp. 14–15, English-medium online copy used because the project Volume 09 scan was unreadable; Sahapedia, A Brief Introduction to Bhavai; Gujarati Vishwakosh, Asait and Gujarat: Fine Arts to Mass Media, theatre section. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Bhavai and the Foundations of Gujarati Theatre

body:
Why Bombay became an important theatre centre

During the 19th century, Bombay developed into a major commercial and cultural centre. Its growing urban population, merchant communities, educational institutions and exposure to European entertainment encouraged the establishment of organised theatrical performances.

The Parsi community played a pioneering role in developing this urban theatrical culture. Gujarati was widely used among Parsis, and many early Parsi theatrical productions were presented in Gujarati.

The beginning of Parsi-Gujarati theatre

An early performance of a Shakespearean play in Gujarati at Surat is recorded in accounts of theatre history in 1852.

In 1853, Framjee Gustadjee Dalal established the Parsi Natak Mandali in Bombay. Its early production of Rustam Sohrab at the Grant Road Theatre is conventionally regarded as a landmark in the emergence of modern Parsi-Gujarati theatre.

The story of Rustam and Sohrab was derived from the Persian epic Shahnameh, composed by the Persian poet Ferdowsi. A short comic play called Dhanji Gharak was also associated with this early performance.

Characteristics of Parsi theatre

  • Organised theatrical companies presenting plays before paying audiences.
  • Stories drawn from Persian legends, Indian mythology, history, social life and Western literature.
  • Prominent use of songs, music and emotionally powerful dialogue.
  • Use of theatre buildings, stage curtains, scenery and costumes.
  • Travel between cities to reach larger audiences.
  • Performances in Gujarati and, as the tradition expanded, languages including Urdu and Hindustani.

The Parsi stage became an important model for professional theatre in several Indian languages. However, Parsi theatre and Gujarati theatre are not identical categories. Parsi theatre identifies a particular historical theatrical tradition, whereas Gujarati theatre includes all theatrical activity in the Gujarati language.

Natak Uttejak Mandali

An important development occurred in 1875, when Ranchhodbhai Udayram Dave and the Parsi literary figure Kaikhushru Kabraji collaborated in establishing the Natak Uttejak Mandali.

Ranchhodbhai's Harishchandra was its inaugural production. His Nal Damayanti also became associated with the company. These productions helped attract Gujarati Hindu audiences to organised theatre and demonstrated the popularity of Indian mythological subjects on the Parsi-influenced stage.

Emergence of Gujarati-owned theatre companies

Gujarati teachers and theatre enthusiasts subsequently sought to establish a company of their own. Ranchhodbhai supported their efforts and prepared his social play Lalita Dukhdarshak for performance.

The Gujarati Natak Mandali was established in Bombay in 1878. In the same year, the Arya Subodh Natak Mandali emerged in Morbi, representing the growth of organised Gujarati theatre within Gujarat itself.

Distinguish the historical milestones

The year 1852 refers to an early recorded Gujarati-language performance at Surat. The year 1853 marks the pioneering Parsi company and its landmark Bombay production. The year 1878 marks the establishment of important Gujarati-owned theatre companies. These are different developments rather than competing dates for the origin of Bhavai or Gujarati dramatic literature.

Prelims focus

  • 1853: Parsi Natak Mandali and Rustam Sohrab.
  • Grant Road Theatre: Bombay.
  • Rustam Sohrab: Persian epic Shahnameh by Ferdowsi.
  • 1875: Natak Uttejak Mandali.
  • 1878: Gujarati Natak Mandali in Bombay and Arya Subodh Natak Mandali in Morbi.
  • Trap: Parsi theatre was not restricted exclusively to the Gujarati language.

[References: Times of India, First Gujarati Theatre Group Came Up in 1878, 27 March 2013; New Indian Express, The Parsi Show Must Go On, archive article; Gujarati Vishwakosh, Ranchhodbhai Udayram Dave and Mumbai Gujarati Natak Mandali; D. G. Vyas, Gujarati Drama, Indian Drama, Publications Division, Government of India, November 1956, pp. 52–60. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

body:
Dalpatram: Early Gujarati dramatic literature

Dalpatram Dahyabhai Travadi (1820–1898) was an important poet and social reformer of 19th-century Gujarat. His dramatic works occupy a foundational position in the development of modern Gujarati literature.

Lakshmi (1850)

Lakshmi, also known as Lakshmi Natak, is conventionally recognised as the first modern Gujarati play in literary histories. It was based on Plutus, a comedy by the ancient Greek playwright Aristophanes.

Dalpatram became familiar with the story through Alexander Kinloch Forbes and adapted it into Gujarati. Although its story originated in Greek literature, its presentation reflected familiarity with Gujarati folk traditions.

The work illustrates an important distinction: the earliest modern Gujarati dramatic text was an adaptation rather than an entirely original dramatic composition.

Mithyabhiman

Mithyabhiman, meaning false pride, is Dalpatram's original social comedy. It was composed around 1870 and published in 1871 by the Gujarat Vernacular Society under the title Mithyabhiman Athva Jivram Bhatt.

The principal character, Jivram Bhatt, is a proud and pretentious man who suffers from night blindness but attempts to conceal his weakness. Through his behaviour and the resulting humorous situations, Dalpatram exposes hypocrisy, arrogance and social pretence.

The play combines elements of Sanskrit drama, Gujarati Bhavai and modern Western theatre. The character Ranglo connects it particularly strongly with Bhavai. Dalpatram described the work as a Bhavai without the Bhungal.

In 1953, Ahmedabad's Natmandal presented a successful production of the play, with Pransukh Nayak playing Jivram Bhatt.

Other early dramatic writing

Early Gujarati drama also included Gulab (1862) by Nagindas Marfatia and Bhatt Nu Bhopalu (1867) by Navalram Pandya. The latter was influenced by the French playwright Moliere. These works demonstrate the growing influence of Indian and European dramatic literature on Gujarati authors.

Ranchhodbhai Udayram Dave

Ranchhodbhai Udayram Dave (1837–1923), born at Mahudha in Kheda district, is commonly regarded as the father of Gujarati drama and theatre.

He sought to make theatre an effective medium of entertainment, moral education and social reform. He opposed what he regarded as excessive vulgarity in contemporary folk performances and encouraged the presentation of well-developed Gujarati plays.

Unlike a writer concerned only with publication, Ranchhodbhai actively participated in the establishment and development of theatrical companies. His association with Natak Uttejak Mandali and Gujarati Natak Mandali helped connect Gujarati literature with professional stage performance.

Important works

WorkYear associated with the textImportance
Jaykumari Vijay1864Early dramatic work
Lalita Dukhdarshak1866Social tragedy
Harishchandra1871Mythological drama concerning truth and duty
Taramati Swayamvar1871Mythological drama
Natyaprakash1890Work on drama and theatre

Lalita Dukhdarshak

Lalita Dukhdarshak is recognised as the first Gujarati tragic play. It portrays the suffering of a woman in an unsuitable marriage and uses her misfortune to expose harmful social customs.

The play was written in 1866 and became a landmark stage production of the Gujarati Natak Mandali in 1878. Its importance lies in bringing a serious contemporary social problem before the theatre-going public.

Three different pioneering associations

  • Asait Thakar: traditional founder of Bhavai.
  • Dalpatram: pioneer of modern Gujarati dramatic literature through Lakshmi and Mithyabhiman.
  • Ranchhodbhai Udayram Dave: father of Gujarati drama and organised Gujarati theatre.

Prelims focus

  • Lakshmi (1850): Dalpatram; adapted from Aristophanes' Plutus.
  • Mithyabhiman: original social comedy by Dalpatram; published in 1871.
  • Jivram Bhatt: protagonist of Mithyabhiman.
  • Ranchhodbhai Udayram Dave: father of Gujarati drama and theatre.
  • Lalita Dukhdarshak: first Gujarati tragedy; written in 1866 and staged by Gujarati Natak Mandali in 1878.
  • Trap: The date of writing a play need not be the date of its first major stage production.

[References: Gujarati Vishwakosh, Kavi Dalpatram, Mithyabhiman, Jivram Bhatt, Ranchhodbhai Udayram Dave and Gujarat: Religion, Culture, Gujarati Language and Literature; Gujarati Vishwakosh, Gujarat: Fine Arts to Mass Media, theatre section; The Wire, How Parsi Theatre Gave an Impetus to Hindu Mythological Plays in Victorian India. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Dalpatram and Ranchhodbhai Udayram Dave: Pioneers of Gujarati Drama

body:
The role of professional theatre companies

A Natak Mandali is an organised theatrical troupe or company. During the late 19th and early 20th centuries, professional Gujarati theatre developed through companies that employed actors, commissioned playwrights, arranged musical productions and presented plays in different towns and cities.

These companies created a continuing market for Gujarati drama. Bombay, Ahmedabad, Surat, Vadodara, Morbi and Wankaner became important centres of theatrical activity.

The period is commonly associated with the Juni Rangbhumi, meaning the old Gujarati stage. Mythological, historical, romantic and social plays were all represented in its repertoire.

Gujarati Natak Mandali and Mumbai Gujarati Natak Mandali

The Gujarati Natak Mandali was established on 5 June 1878 in Bombay, with the support of Ranchhodbhai Udayram Dave. Its early success was associated with Lalita Dukhdarshak.

After the original company encountered difficulties, Dayashankar Vasanji Girnara acquired it and established the Shri Mumbai Gujarati Natak Mandali in 1889.

The inaugural production of the reorganised company was Kulin Kanta, based on Kanta by Manilal Nabhubhai Dwivedi. It was presented on 29 June 1889.

The company became a leading institution of the old Gujarati stage. It was associated with playwright Mulshankar Mulani, actor Jayshankar Sundari, actor-director Bapulal Nayak and several important musical productions.

Its repertoire included Saubhagya Sundari, Mulani's Ajabkumari and Ramanbhai Nilkanth's Rai No Parvat. The company's historical period is generally given as 1889–1948.

The Gujarati Natak Mandali of 1878 and the Mumbai Gujarati Natak Mandali of 1889 were historically connected institutions, but their establishment dates should not be interchanged.

Deshi Natak Samaj

The Deshi Natak Samaj was established in Ahmedabad in 1889 and is particularly associated with Dahyabhai Dholashaji Zaveri. Keshavlal Shivram's musical play Sangeet Lilavati, based on a Jain narrative, played an important role in the company's formation.

Dahyabhai contributed as a playwright, director, composer and theatre entrepreneur. The company's early repertoire included Sati Sanyukta, Vir Vikramaditya, Ashrumati and Veenaveli.

The company moved its operations to Bombay in 1896. It subsequently developed a theatre of its own and became closely identified with Bhangwadi Theatre in the Kalbadevi area of Bombay.

The company's later successes included Prabhulal Dwivedi's Vadilona Vanke (1938) and Same Paar (1947). The institution continued until 1980, making it one of the longest-lived companies in Gujarati theatre history.

Other important theatre companies

CompanyEstablishmentKey association
Arya Subodh Natak Mandali1878, MorbiMulji Oza, Vaghji Oza; Bharthari
Arya Naitik Natak Samaj1915, VadodaraNakubhai Kalubhai Shah; Baliwala Grand Theatre, Bombay
Laxmikant Natak Samaj1917Chandulal Hargovandas Shah; Prabhulal Dwivedi's plays

The Morbi Arya Subodh Natak Mandali achieved early recognition through its production of Bharthari. It represents the growth of professional theatre in Saurashtra rather than its concentration exclusively in Bombay.

Laxmikant Natak Samaj became particularly prominent through productions such as Arunodaya, Malavpati Munj, Prithviraj and Sirajuddaula.

A successful play could be performed by several companies over time. Therefore, an association between a play and one company does not necessarily mean that the play was never staged by another company.

Prelims focus

  • 1878: Gujarati Natak Mandali and Arya Subodh Natak Mandali.
  • 1889: Mumbai Gujarati Natak Mandali and Deshi Natak Samaj.
  • Dayashankar Vasanji Girnara: Mumbai Gujarati Natak Mandali.
  • Dahyabhai Dholashaji Zaveri: Deshi Natak Samaj.
  • Bhangwadi Theatre: Deshi Natak Samaj.
  • 1917: Laxmikant Natak Samaj, associated with Prabhulal Dwivedi.

[References: Gujarati Vishwakosh, Mumbai Gujarati Natak Mandali, Deshi Natak Samaj, Dahyabhai Dholashaji, Manilal Nabhubhai Dwivedi, Arya Naitik Natak Samaj and Laxmikant Natak Samaj; Times of India, First Gujarati Theatre Group Came Up in 1878, 27 March 2013. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]
